title: Publish only after the quality gate: make dependencies carry the rule
goal: Model a pipeline as a DAG where publish waits for validated data and cleanup still runs after failure.
concept:
A restaurant does not serve a plate before the safety check. A data workflow needs the same rule: publish depends on validation succeeding.

A directed acyclic graph, or DAG, records those prerequisites. It allows independent work to run together, but it prevents the final step from starting early.
example:
Batch B21 lands 1,000 rows. The quality task finds 12 invalid customer IDs. A correct graph blocks publish, records the failed gate, and still runs cleanup or notification.

The green “ingest succeeded” signal is not enough. The business outcome is whether only validated rows become visible.

use_case.when: Use task dependencies when later work is unsafe or meaningless until named prerequisites finish.
use_case.example: Ingest sales, validate keys, publish a gold table only after validation, and notify after the graph finishes.
use_case.decision: Use a DAG for durable, observable multi-step work. Keep one atomic SQL transaction when all changes fit one database and one short unit of work.

practice: Choose whether B21 passes validation. Predict which nodes run and which table customers can query.
boundary: The browser models task state only. It does not schedule compute, persist checkpoints, retry tasks, charge credits, or reproduce either vendor runtime.
js:
function dagPaint(){const pass=qualityOutcome.value==='pass';world.innerHTML='

Visible gold rows: '+(pass?'1,000':'0')+'. Cleanup/notification still records the outcome.

';}qualityOutcome.onchange=dagPaint;dagPaint();
questions: Validation fails for B21. What should publish do?
The dependency is the business gate, not a timing hint.
Why keep a finalizer or failure handler?
To record/clean up after either outcome
Terminal handling is different from publishing business data.
A single short database transaction can enforce the whole change
Do not replace one atomic unit with distributed orchestration without a reason.

steps.note: Record the two observed task outcomes.

steps.code: result={"publish":"success" if can_publish else "blocked","finalize":"failure" if "failed" in tasks.values() else "success"}
steps.note: Derive business publish and terminal handling separately.

walkthrough.limit: Executed local Python over synthetic states; no vendor scheduler or SQL ran.

visual_explanation: Follow the green ingest node to the quality gate. The publish edge changes from blocked to allowed; the finalizer remains reachable in both outcomes.
written_questions: Which business invariant should your publish task enforce?
What state must be preserved before retrying a failed task graph?

product_sections.title: Databricks: Lakeflow Jobs dependencies and Run if
product_sections.html:
Use case. Keep a gold-table publish task behind a data-quality task while a failure handler records bad batches.

Prepared real lab. Use an authorized non-production Databricks workspace and job identity with permissions to manage/run the job. Compute and task runs can incur cost.

Why this is not SQL first. This is job control, so the example uses declarative job YAML. The SQL belongs inside the tasks; there is no SQL statement in this lesson that creates the Lakeflow Jobs DAG.

The YAML is not applied in Databricks. Buttons replay a local state model.

- task_key: validate- task_key: publish
  depends_on: [{task_key: validate}]
  run_if: ALL_SUCCESS- task_key: notify_failure
  depends_on: [{task_key: validate}]
  run_if: AT_LEAST_ONE_FAILED

Failure/fix. ALL_SUCCESS blocks publish after validation failure. A separate failure task handles notification. Excluded/upstream-failed states have documented rules, so test the exact branch.

Authorized non-production workspace; YAML unexecuted. Job control uses YAML here because SQL does not define this Lakeflow Jobs dependency graph.

```yaml

  depends_on: [{task_key: validate}]
  run_if: ALL_SUCCESS
- task_key: notify_failure
  depends_on: [{task_key: validate}]

```

The local model shows publish blocked and failure notification selected.

product_sections.title: Snowflake: CREATE TASK … AFTER and one finalizer
product_sections.html:
Use case. Express the same quality gate as a Snowflake task graph, using SQL DDL.

Prepared real lab. Use an authorized non-production database/schema, a task-owning role, and either serverless tasks or a warehouse. Ownership, warehouse usage, and task execution can incur cost.

The SQL is not run on Snowflake. Buttons replay a local state model.

CREATE TASK ingest SCHEDULE='USING CRON 0 * * * * UTC' AS CALL load_b21();CREATE TASK validate AFTER ingest AS CALL assert_b21_quality();
CREATE TASK publish AFTER validate AS CALL publish_b21();CREATE TASK finish FINALIZE = ingest AS CALL record_graph_result();

Failure/fix. A child with multiple parents waits for successful predecessors; a finalizer runs after other tasks finish or fail. Snowflake documents graph ownership, limits, resume steps, and retry behavior—DDL creation alone does not activate a production graph.

title: Publish one configuration snapshot, not three changing fields
goal: Let every request observe one complete configuration version instead of an impossible mixture.
concept:
Imagine replacing a restaurant menu one page at a time while customers are ordering. A reader can combine prices from the old menu with rules from the new one.

Build a complete immutable configuration, then publish one reference to it. Each request reads that reference once. The formal mechanism is an atomic snapshot publication.
example: Version 1 is {timeout:1000, retries:2, route:A}. Version 2 is {timeout:400, retries:0, route:B}. Three separate field writes can expose {1000,0,B}, a version that never existed. One AtomicReference<Config> yields either v1 or v2.

use_case.when: Use this when many request threads read related configuration fields while a control-plane thread refreshes them.
use_case.example: Publish routing, timeout, and retry policy together in a Java service after validating the full update.
use_case.decision: Use an immutable snapshot for coherent read-mostly state. Use locks or a database transaction when readers must coordinate mutations, not only observe a version.

practice: Switch from separate fields to one snapshot and move the reader between update steps. Find the impossible mixed version.
boundary: The browser fixes one interleaving. Atomic publication does not validate configuration, coordinate external systems, or make mutable objects inside the snapshot safe.

function configPaint(){const snap=configMode.value==='snapshot',m=readMoment.value;let v;if(snap)v=m==='before'?['1000','2','A']:['400','0','B'];else v=m==='before'?['1000','2','A']:m==='middle'?['1000','0','B']:['400','0','B'];const mixed=v.join('/')!=='1000/2/A'&&v.join('/')!=='400/0/B';world.innerHTML='
timeout '+v[0]+' ms
retries '+v[1]+'
route '+v[2]+'

'+(mixed?'Impossible mixture: no validated version had these values.':'Coherent version observed.')+'

';}configMode.onchange=configPaint;readMoment.onchange=configPaint;configPaint();
questions: Reader sees {1000,0,B}. What does that prove?
That tuple exists in neither v1 nor v2.
What should a request do with the AtomicReference?
Call get once and use that Config
One read pins one coherent version for that decision.
The snapshot is local process state, not a distributed transaction.

steps.code:
record Config(int timeoutMs, int retries, String route) {}
var config=new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference<>(new Config(1000,2,"A"));

steps.note: Publish v2 with one atomic reference write.

walkthrough.limit: Executed on local Java 17. It demonstrates reference publication, not a race detector or a distributed configuration service.

sources: Java SE 25 concurrent package memory consistency
visual_explanation: The three field boxes can show a tuple that never existed. Snapshot mode restricts the visual to exactly v1 or v2.
written_questions: Which fields in your service must change as one version?
What mutable object would accidentally weaken an “immutable” snapshot?

title: An architecture rule that cannot fail the build is only advice
goal: Turn one high-value architecture constraint into an executable fitness function with an owner and exception path.
concept:
Incident. A deployment was green, but a new customer-data bucket was public and unencrypted. The review checklist said “private and encrypted”; nobody executed the check.

A fitness function turns an architecture outcome into a repeatable test. It does not test everything. It makes one important boundary hard to cross accidentally.
example:
The manifest says classification=PII, public=true, encrypted=false. The deployment job itself succeeds—our misleading green signal. The fitness function emits two violations and blocks promotion until both fields change or a time-bounded exception is approved.

Trigger: a new manifest. Mechanism: unenforced prose. Impact: exposed regulated data. Missing control: a pre-deployment policy test.

use_case.when: Use fitness functions when a cross-team architecture rule is objective, important, and cheap enough to evaluate repeatedly.
use_case.example: Block a PII data product unless storage is private, encrypted, and owned.
use_case.decision: Automate deterministic constraints. Keep nuanced tradeoffs in human review, and provide explicit, expiring exceptions instead of hidden bypasses.

practice: Change classification, encryption, and exposure. Predict the exact rule failures and whether promotion is blocked.
boundary: This local rules engine checks three synthetic fields. Real controls need authoritative inventory, identity, policy versioning, exception expiry, and evidence that deployed state matches the manifest.

function fitnessPaint(){const pii=classification.value==='PII',errs=[];if(pii&&encrypted.value!=='yes')errs.push('PII must be encrypted');if(pii&&exposure.value!=='private')errs.push('PII must be private');world.innerHTML='
Build
SUCCESS
Architecture gate
'+(errs.length?'BLOCK':'PASS')+'
'+(errs.length?errs.join('
'):'No selected violation')+'
';}classification.onchange=fitnessPaint;encrypted.onchange=fitnessPaint;exposure.onchange=fitnessPaint;fitnessPaint();
questions: Build is green but PII is public. Senior response?
Add an executable pre-deploy rule at the boundary
The missing mechanism is enforcement, not awareness.
Which is a good fitness function?
“PII storage must be private and encrypted”
When should the gate not decide alone?
A nuanced tradeoff with incomplete evidence
Judgment-heavy decisions need accountable human review.

steps.note: Make the promotion decision from evidence.

written_questions: Which one architecture rule would prevent your most expensive recurring exception?
Who owns expiry and audit of an approved exception?

title: Freeze the tool catalog: schema drift can impersonate model drift
goal: Record the exact tool schemas used by every evaluation so a changed harness is not blamed on the model.
concept:
Two runners take the same exam, but one receives a calculator with different buttons. Comparing their scores as if the exam were identical is unfair.

An agent evaluation includes the model, prompt, data, and tool catalog. Tool names, descriptions, input schemas, and output schemas can change. Snapshot a canonical catalog and hash it for every trial.
example: Trial A exposes search(query). Trial B exposes search(query, region required). The same agent call now fails validation. Without a catalog hash, the dashboard says “model regression”; the evidence actually says “harness changed.”

use_case.when: Use catalog snapshots when comparing models, prompts, or releases that can call MCP tools.
use_case.example: Store canonical tools/list output, protocol version, server build, and schema hash with each eval trial.
use_case.decision: Pin tools for controlled comparisons. Run a separate compatibility suite against the live catalog so production drift is still detected.

practice: Switch the second trial between the same and changed tool schema. Decide whether the score difference is attributable.
boundary: The browser uses two tiny schemas and a displayed teaching hash. Production canonicalization must define ordering, omit volatile fields deliberately, retain full schemas securely, and include server/protocol identity.

search(query)
score 1
Trial B
hash '+(same?'6a1f':'9c42')+'
search(query'+(same?'':', region!')+')
score '+(same?'1':'0')+'

'+(same?'Controlled comparison: tool contract held constant.':'Confounded comparison: schema changed with the score.')+'

';}catalogB.onchange=catalogPaint;catalogPaint();
questions: Same prompt/model, different tool hash, lower score. First conclusion?
The harness changed with the measured outcome.
What belongs in the trial record?
Catalog snapshot/hash plus model, prompt, data and protocol/server versions
Attribution needs the effective environment, not secrets.
Why still test the live catalog?
Production tools can drift and need separate compatibility evidence
Controlled evaluation and production compatibility answer different questions.

written_questions: Which volatile catalog fields should your canonicalizer exclude, and why?
What separate test proves a pinned agent still works with today’s live tools?

title: Three probability maps, one mask: ensemble confidence is not independent evidence
goal: Understand probability averaging, its reported benefit, and the correlated-error boundary in a recent vision study.
concept:
Three weather forecasters can average their rain probabilities. That often steadies a noisy forecast—but not when all three rely on the same broken sensor.

A recent panoramic street-segmentation study averaged class probabilities across independently seeded models and multiple views. Averaging changes confidence before the final class choice.
example:
For one pixel, three models assign “road” probabilities 0.90, 0.80, and 0.20. The mean is 0.63, so a 0.50 threshold labels road. If all three share the same blind spot and output 0.10, agreement is confidently wrong.

The paper reports 60.95% mean IoU on an 84-image public validation split and 57.08% on the hidden test leaderboard. Those are study results, not a universal production guarantee.

use_case.when: Potentially useful when prediction quality justifies extra inference cost and independently trained models make meaningfully different errors.
use_case.example: Average per-class probabilities from three segmentation seeds before producing a street-scene mask.
use_case.decision: Measure hidden-set gain, latency, memory, calibration, and error correlation. Prefer one model when ensemble cost exceeds the verified benefit.

practice: Choose diverse or correlated model outputs and move the decision threshold. Predict the pixel label and confidence.
boundary: This one-pixel model omits spatial structure, class imbalance, calibration, multi-scale transforms, mIoU aggregation, and the paper’s full implementation. It does not reproduce the study.

Mean road probability: '+avg.toFixed(2)+' → '+(avg>=t?'ROAD':'NOT ROAD')+'

'+(ensembleCase.value==='wrong'?'Agreement did not create independent evidence.':'Different outputs were averaged before thresholding.')+'

';}ensembleCase.onchange=ensemblePaint;threshold.oninput=ensemblePaint;ensemblePaint();

All seeds share one training blind spot. What can happen?
Diversity of seeds is not proof of independent errors.
What limits the paper’s reported metrics?
They come from specified validation/hidden challenge data and workflow
Research claims transfer only with matching evidence.

title: Do not run fork code inside a trusted pull_request_target job
goal: Keep untrusted pull-request code out of jobs that hold base-repository secrets or write tokens.
concept:
A visitor may hand reception a form. They should not be allowed to replace the receptionist’s instruction book and then use the master keys.

pull_request is designed to run untrusted fork code with restrictions. pull_request_target runs trusted base-branch workflow logic with elevated trust. The dangerous combination is checking out the fork head and then executing it in that trusted job.
example:
A workflow triggered by pull_request_target checks out github.event.pull_request.head.sha and runs make test. The PR changes the Makefile to print a secret. Checkout alone is data movement; make test completes the exploit by executing attacker-controlled code.

GitHub’s current guide says its default public-repository policy is in evaluate mode and is scheduled for enforcement on November 2, 2026. Verify policy state again before relying on that date.

use_case.when: Use this distinction for public repositories accepting fork pull requests, especially when workflows can write, use secrets, populate caches, or reach internal runners.
use_case.example: Run tests on pull_request with read-only permissions; perform trusted labeling separately without executing fork code.
use_case.decision: Prefer pull_request for building/testing fork code. Use pull_request_target only for necessary trusted automation and keep PR content as untrusted data.

practice: Choose the event, whether fork code is executed, and whether secrets are present. Locate the trust-boundary crossing.
boundary: This model reduces GitHub’s permission, approval, cache, artifact, runner, and policy system to three switches. Review current organization policies and the complete secure-use guidance.
js:
function trustPaint(){const privileged=eventKind.value==='target'&&secretAccess.value==='yes',exec=runFork.value==='yes',risk=privileged&&exec;world.innerHTML='

'+(risk?'PWN REQUEST PATH':'No modeled secret-execution crossing')+'

';}eventKind.onchange=trustPaint;runFork.onchange=trustPaint;secretAccess.onchange=trustPaint;trustPaint();
questions: What completes the vulnerable pattern after checking out fork code?
Execution gives attacker-controlled files the job’s authority.
Safer default for fork tests without secrets?
The pull_request event applies fork protections.
Does “checkout only” make all later steps safe?
No; tools may execute checked-out scripts, dependencies, or config
Execution can be indirect. Follow the data into every tool.

steps.note: Detect untrusted execution with elevated authority.
Fail the policy check before the job runs.

walkthrough.limit: Executed local policy arithmetic only; it did not run GitHub Actions or process real repository secrets.

sources: Living documentation with a dated 2026-11-02 policy milestone
visual_explanation: The arrow is harmless data inspection until it becomes execution inside the privileged zone; then the destination box turns red.
written_questions: Which current workflow could execute fork-controlled configuration indirectly?
How would you separate untrusted testing from a later trusted action?

title: Retry-After is a floor, not a synchronized alarm clock
goal: Use 429/503 plus Retry-After to slow clients without creating a retry herd or duplicating unsafe work.
concept:
A crowded café asks customers to return after three minutes. If everyone sets the same alarm, the doorway floods again at exactly minute three.

Retry-After tells a client how long it ought to wait before a follow-up request. A robust client respects that minimum, then may add bounded jitter so many clients do not synchronize.
example:
Five clients receive 429 Too Many Requests and Retry-After: 3. Immediate retry sends five more requests at second 1. Exact retry moves all five to second 3. Respecting the three-second floor and adding bounded jitter spreads them across seconds 3–5.

Timing does not make a non-idempotent payment safe to repeat. Retry permission and operation semantics are separate decisions.

use_case.when: Use this when an API enforces quotas or is temporarily unavailable and clients can retry safely.
use_case.example: An ingestion API returns 429 with Retry-After: 3; SDK clients wait at least three seconds and add bounded jitter.
use_case.decision: Retry safe/idempotent operations within a deadline. Require an idempotency mechanism or explicit status lookup before repeating side-effecting requests.

practice: Compare immediate, exact, and jittered schedules for five clients. Notice load concentration and the earliest retry.
boundary: The teaching schedule uses whole seconds and fixed jitter. Real clients must parse HTTP-date or delay-seconds, account for clocks and deadlines, cap attempts, and observe operation semantics.

'+t+'s'+Array.from({length:n},(_,i)=>'C'+(times.slice(0,times.indexOf(t)+i+1).length)+'').join('')+'
';}world.innerHTML='
'+cells+'

Earliest retry: '+Math.min(...times)+'s. Peak simultaneous retries: '+Math.max(...Object.values(times.reduce((m,t)=>(m[t]=(m[t]||0)+1,m),{})))+'.

'+(mode==='immediate'?'Violates the 3-second advice.':mode==='exact'?'Compliant, but synchronized.':'Compliant floor with a spread-out retry wave.')+'

';}retryMode.onchange=retryPaint;retryPaint();

The field asks the client to wait.
Why add jitter after the floor?
Jitter reduces the retry herd; it does not change method semantics.
Whether repeating the operation is safe
Timing and idempotency are different boundaries.

steps.note: Record the server floor and bounded client jitter.
Schedule no request before the floor.
